st.t: Aggregate productivity: Task speedups shrink during scaling
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central distinction between task-level speedups and aggregate productivity by translating experimental gains through affected-task and labour-cost shares. Its much higher 6.95% projection does not reject that framework; it illustrates the cluster’s point that aggregate estimates vary sharply with assumptions about future scaling, cross-task transfer, adoption and profitability.
qs: Here a version of Hulten’s theorem is used to estimate aggregate productivity gains based on the fractions of tasks in the economy that are affected by AI and the average task-level cost savings.
This yields an estimate of 6.95% productivity growth over the next decade from LLMs, a significant amount of growth.

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between task-level productivity evidence and broader economic outcomes. It projects substantial aggregate productivity growth from model scaling and inference-cost assumptions, but treats this as a forward-looking estimate and explicitly leaves cross-domain generalisation unresolved; it does not establish improved employment, income or career outcomes.
qs: These changes leads to a significantly higher productivity estimate of around a magnitude higher than in Acemoglu (2024) with an estimate 6.9% productivity growth.
Whether these economic scaling laws generalize to other domains and for greater model training compute sizes is a question for further research.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of meaningful but uneven productivity gains on bounded tasks, including larger gains for lower-skilled users. Its narrow translation experiment and explicit uncertainty about cross-domain generalisation also align with the cluster’s caution against inferring general legal autonomy or realised economy-wide outcomes, though it does not address legal verification or apprenticeship risks directly.
qs: Scaling LLMs therefore leads to gains with significant heterogeneity by participant skill, with lower-skilled participants obtaining the largest gains.
Whether these economic scaling laws generalize to other domains and for greater model training compute sizes is a question for further research.

st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s task-specific, measurement-based framing: pooled AI assistance produced a substantial, statistically significant reduction in translation time, while the modest quality increase was not statistically significant. st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core claim that LLMs can produce substantial task-level productivity gains while effects vary by task, model capability and user skill. Its translation experiment adds controlled evidence of faster completion and larger gains for lower-skilled users, while its explicit limits on cross-domain generalisation align with selective deployment. Its macroeconomic projection is more expansive than the cluster’s legal-work conclusions, but is presented as assumption-dependent rather than proof of general competence or realised legal-sector value.

kp.k: Randomized translation experiment tests economic effects of model scaling
kp.d: Merali's preregistered experiment involved 300 professional translators completing 1,800 tasks, with access to one of 13 LLMs or a no-AI control. Participants translated English into Spanish, Hindi or Arabic, completed an unaided baseline and five subsequent tasks, and received performance incentives. This is evidence about AI-assisted professional translation, rather than a direct study of legal services.
qs: In a preregistered online experi- ment, 300 professional translators completed 1,800 tasks using one of 13 LLMs (or a control).
The participants then completed five more tasks during the experiment.
All participants completed a baseline task without any AI assistance offering a metric for translator skill.

kp.k: Pooled AI access substantially reduces task completion time
kp.d: Pooling all 13 models, the paper reports that average completion time fell from 600.7 seconds without AI to 413.8 seconds with AI, a 31.1% reduction (reported p=0.000). Mean quality increased from 4.51 to 4.71 on a seven-point scale, equivalent to 0.14 standard deviations, but this pooled quality difference was not statistically significant (p=0.148).
qs: With access to any AI model this was reduced to 413.8 seconds (p=0.000), a statistically significant reduction in time of 31.1%.
The average grade without access to an AI model was 4.51.
When participants were able to use an AI model this increased to 4.71, an increase of 0.2 points on a seven-point scale.

kp.k: Greater training compute improves speed and quality
kp.d: The main text reports that each tenfold increase in model training compute reduced completion time by 12.3% (p=0.001) and increased quality by 0.25 points on a seven-point scale, or 0.18 standard deviations (reported p=0.000). The author translates a roughly 70-fold compute increase, termed a 'GPT-jump', into a 22.7% time reduction and a 0.33-standard-deviation grade improvement. These are estimated scaling relationships in assisted translation, not findings about all professional tasks.
qs: For every 10x increase in model training compute, translator’s managed to complete a task 12.3% quicker (p=0.001).
For every 10x in- crease in model compute grades improved by 0.25 points on a 7-point scale or by 0.18 standard deviations (p=0.000).

kp.k: Incentive-adjusted earnings rise with model training compute
kp.d: The preferred preregistered productivity measure was earnings per minute, including quality bonuses. Participants received $10 for satisfactory completion of all six tasks and could earn $2 per high-quality task, defined by an average expert grade of at least six out of seven. Average earnings were $1.18 per minute; each tenfold compute increase added approximately $0.19 per minute, reported as a 16.1% gain (p=0.001), or 29.7% per GPT-jump. This outcome measures experimental compensation, not market wages.
qs: The above results set the stage for the preferred pre-registered metric for task productivity, earnings per minute.
The average participant earned $1.18 per minute of completing tasks.
This increased by $0.19 a minute for every 10x increase in compute the model they received was given in training (p=0.001).

kp.k: Slower baseline translators benefit more from larger models
kp.d: The study classified participants as high-skill or low-skill using below- or above-median unaided baseline completion time. Per tenfold compute increase, the high-skill group reduced time by 4.9%, versus 21.1% for the low-skill group, with a reported heterogeneity p-value of 0.017. Corresponding GPT-jump reductions were 9% and 39.0%. Merali suggests implications for skill-biased technological change and wage inequality, rather than reporting observed changes in labor-market wage inequality.
qs: Those who completed the baseline task in below median time were classed as high-skill whilst though who took above median time were classed as low-skill.
In particular, whilst high-skilled participants reduce their time taken by 4.9% for every 10x increase in compute those with low- skill have a 21.1% reduction (p=0.017).
These translate into 9% and 39.0% reductions in time taken per ’GPT-Jump’.

kp.k: Macroeconomic projection assumes transferable relative scaling gains
kp.d: Adapting Acemoglu's Hulten-theorem framework, Merali retains 19.9% AI task exposure and a 0.57 labor share but adjusts assumed productivity effects for model improvement. He does not assume identical scaling laws across tasks; instead, he assumes translation's ratio between initial AI gains and subsequent scaling gains transfers to other tasks. On that basis, he projects that studies reporting 14% and 40% gains would yield 25.5% and 54.9% with the largest currently available models, averaging 40.2%. Assuming models trained with approximately 10^30 FLOPs become commercially available by 2030 and subsequently diffuse, projected effects become 39.1% and 84.4%, averaging 61.2%. These are extrapolations, not replications.
qs: Note we do not assume that the scaling laws for different tasks all follow those of the scaling laws for translation- other tasks may see differential productivity gains.
This yields an average of a 61.2% productivity effect in ten years time when we account for (both past and) future model scaling, compared to the original 27% estimate.

kp.k: Low inference costs underpin assumed universal economic feasibility
kp.d: Merali rejects applying a computer-vision-based estimate that only 23% of automatable tasks would be economically feasible within ten years to LLM-assisted work. He reports total inference spending significantly below one dollar for the experiment's AI-assisted tasks and assumes that any task on which an LLM improves productivity will be profitable to assist. He acknowledges that professional interaction time is much more costly than inference, but says the time-based productivity estimates already include it.
qs: For this domain therefore, the profitable automation rate would be roughly 100%.
This means that for the purpose of this calculation we assume that if LLMs can increase productivity on a task it will always be profitable.

kp.k: Projected aggregate productivity growth depends on restrictive assumptions
kp.d: Multiplying 19.9% task exposure, a projected 61.2% task-level productivity effect and a 57% labor share produces the paper's 6.95% US productivity-growth estimate over the next decade. The calculation holds economic task structure and the rate of technological progress unchanged. Merali suggests the estimate could be a lower bound if AI accelerates scientific discovery; this is a conditional argument, not an experimentally established aggregate outcome.
qs: This yields an estimate of 6.95% productivity growth over the next decade from LLMs, a significant amount of growth.
For in- stance, it is assumed that the task structure of the economy doesn’t change at all despite significant technological changes.
Further, and of particular significance, it also assumes no change to the rate of technological progress itself.

kp.k: Generalization beyond short translation tasks remains untested
kp.d: The author explicitly limits the evidence to one professional skill, short tasks and just over two orders of magnitude of training compute. Generalization to other domains and larger models remains a research question. Legal-task productivity gains are cited from prior research, not measured in this experiment; the paper therefore supplies cross-domain evidence about augmentation and differential worker gains rather than direct findings about legal staffing, pricing or regulation.
qs: Further, the results were only derived on a range of just over two orders of magnitude of compute.
Whether these economic scaling laws generalize to other domains and for greater model training compute sizes is a question for further research.

Previous research has already highlighted the potential for currently avail- able LLMs to offer double-digit productivity improvements in a wide range of settings including legal tasks, consulting, software engineering, and a variety of professional tasks.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Merali claims that LLM assistance improves professional translation productivity, that larger models yield greater gains, and that slower baseline performers benefit most. He projects approximately 6.95% aggregate US productivity growth from LLMs over the following decade.
pts.d: In this cross-domain source, the original findings concern human translators assisted by AI, not legal services or autonomous replacement of professionals. Pooling all 13 models, Merali reports a 31.1% reduction in task time, from 600.7 to 413.8 seconds. Average quality rises from 4.51 to 4.71 out of seven, but the pooled quality difference is not statistically significant (p=0.148). Across model training-compute levels, he reports 12.3% less task time, 0.25 additional grade points (0.18 standard deviations), and 16.1% higher earnings per minute per tenfold increase in compute. His approximately 70-fold 'GPT-jump' corresponds to reported improvements of 22.7% in task time, 0.33 standard deviations in grades, and 29.7% in earnings per minute. Participants classified as lower-skilled by baseline completion time have a 21.1% time reduction per tenfold compute increase, versus 4.9% among higher-skilled participants. He suggests implications for skill-related wage inequality, without measuring subsequent market wages. His economy-wide estimate is a conditional extrapolation, not an experimental finding. References to legal productivity improvements summarize earlier research rather than establish new legal-sector results.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The translation claims rest on a preregistered randomized experiment; the macroeconomic prediction combines its results with external estimates and explicit extrapolation assumptions.
pts.d: Merali reports recruiting 300 professional translators through Freelancer and Fiverr, evenly divided among Spanish, Hindi and Arabic. Participants completed 1,800 tasks including an unassisted baseline task each, followed by five experimental tasks with one of 13 assigned models or no AI. The pooled time regressions use 1,500 observations; compute regressions generally use 1,392, with slightly fewer quality observations. Three experienced professional translators graded submissions. Participants received $10 for completion and could earn $2 per high-quality task, making earnings per minute an experimental, incentive-dependent productivity measure rather than an observed market wage. The paper reports p=0.001 for the headline time and earnings scaling estimates, p=0.000 for quality scaling, and p=0.017 for skill heterogeneity. The macro calculation uses Acemoglu's Hulten-theorem framework, Eloundou et al.'s 19.9% AI-exposed task share, a 57% labor share, and a projected 61.2% task productivity effect. That projected effect rescales earlier call-center and writing studies using translation-derived gain ratios and Epoch AI compute forecasts. Merali also invokes very low experimental inference costs and declining inference prices to assume that all productivity-improving LLM applications are profitable. These are offered as grounds for the projection, not as direct economy-wide experimental evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The observed effects apply to short translation tasks and the tested compute range; the decade-ahead prediction requires continued scaling, adoption, transferable gain ratios and profitability.
pts.d: The December 2024 paper observes task-level outcomes during its experiment, not long-run workplace performance. It tests only translation, on short tasks averaging roughly ten minutes, across just over two orders of magnitude of training compute. Merali expressly leaves generalization to other domains and larger compute scales for further research. His projection covers the next ten years, approximately to 2034, using an assumption that models trained with about 10^30 FLOPs become commercially available by 2030 and that the remaining years allow widespread adoption. It does not assume identical scaling laws across occupations; it assumes that the ratio between initial AI-assistance gains and additional gains from larger models matches translation. The calculation holds the economy's task structure and the underlying rate of technological progress fixed, and assumes productivity-improving LLM use is profitable. Merali characterizes the estimate as potentially a lower bound because AI might also accelerate scientific and technological progress; this is a qualification of his scenario rather than an empirically established minimum.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly studied population is professional translators; broader implications concern workers in AI-exposed tasks and aggregate US productivity, not demonstrated changes to legal employment or legal markets.
pts.d: Participants translated English into Spanish, Hindi or Arabic and had professional translation experience. They used AI as assistance while remaining responsible for completing the tasks. The reported benefits are faster completion, higher graded quality as compute increases, and greater earnings per minute under the study's payment scheme. 'Lower-skilled' means taking above-median time on the unassisted baseline task, not being a junior worker, having fewer qualifications or belonging to an independently established low-skill occupational group. Larger gains for these participants motivate Merali's discussion of possible effects on wage inequality. His macroeconomic extrapolation extends to US workers performing AI-exposed tasks, with call-center and professional-writing studies supplying comparison estimates. Lawyers and other knowledge workers appear as populations studied in prior literature; this experiment does not measure effects on law firms, clients, legal fees, staffing, employment displacement or access to justice.
